cluster.name: Bengaluru
cluster.summary: Karnataka's capital pairs Deccan-era forts and palaces with colonial-era parks, a dense museum circuit and a modern cafe culture. Its 900 m elevation keeps the climate mild year round, making it one of the easiest Indian cities to walk.
cluster.intercity_hub: Kempegowda International Airport (BLR) / KSR Bengaluru City Junction

attractions.name: Lalbagh Botanical Garden
attractions.summary: A 240-acre botanical garden begun by Hyder Ali, best known for its Victorian glass house and a 3,000-million-year-old rock outcrop.
attractions.history: Hyder Ali laid out the garden around 1760 as a Mughal-style pleasure garden, and his son Tipu Sultan expanded it by importing plants from across Asia, Africa and Europe. Under British administration it became a government botanical garden in 1856 and was placed under the Department of Horticulture. The Glass House, modelled on London's Crystal Palace, was built in 1889 to mark the visit of the Prince of Wales, and has hosted the biannual Lalbagh Flower Show ever since.
attractions.significance: Lalbagh is India's most important early example of a princely garden converted to a public botanical institution. Its collection includes rare tropical and subtropical species and one of the country's largest collections of plants gathered under a single colonial-era horticultural programme. The Lalbagh Rock, a peninsular gneiss outcrop, is a designated National Geological Monument.
interesting_facts: The Lalbagh Rock is peninsular gneiss dated to roughly 3,000 million years, among the oldest exposed rock formations on Earth.
One of Kempegowda's four watchtowers, built to mark the boundaries of old Bengaluru, still stands on the rock.
The Glass House was fabricated in Glasgow and shipped to India in sections.
The garden holds a biannual flower show every Republic Day and Independence Day week, drawing lakhs of visitors.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Main tarred loops are flat and wheelchair-friendly; the rock outcrop and several inner trails involve steps and uneven stone. Benches and drinking water are available along the main circuit.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; comfortable walking shoes recommended.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography allowed. Commercial or pre-wedding shoots require prior written permission from the Directorate of Horticulture.
local_customs: Feeding the resident birds and monkeys is discouraged.
Plastic is restricted inside the garden.

schedule.note: Glass House keeps shorter hours than the garden

attractions.verification_note: Entry fee and Glass House timings change during flower-show weeks - verify before visiting.

sources.title: Department of Horticulture, Government of Karnataka

attractions.name: Bangalore Palace
attractions.summary: A Tudor-revival palace of turrets, fortified towers and carved woodwork, built by the Wadiyar rulers of Mysore.
attractions.history: The estate was acquired in 1873 by the Maharaja of Mysore, Chamaraja Wadiyar X, and construction of the present palace was completed in 1878. The design draws directly on English Tudor and Scottish Gothic revival architecture, reportedly inspired by Windsor Castle. It remained a residence of the Wadiyar family and passed through a long ownership dispute with the Karnataka government after the abolition of privy purses.
attractions.significance: The palace is the clearest surviving statement of how the Mysore royal family projected a modern, Anglophile identity in the late nineteenth century, in deliberate contrast with the Indo-Saracenic idiom used at Mysore Palace. Its interiors preserve Wadiyar-era furniture, portraiture and a notable collection of paintings by Raja Ravi Varma.
interesting_facts: The ballroom and Durbar Hall retain their original stained glass and carved rosewood.
The grounds are regularly used as a large concert venue, which occasionally closes parts of the site.
The audio guide included with the ticket is one of the better ones in the city and is available in several languages.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The ground floor is largely step-free; upper floors are reached by staircases with no lift. Staff can advise on the accessible route.
attractions.photography_policy: Still photography requires a separate paid camera ticket. Tripods and commercial shoots need advance permission.
local_customs: Footwear is permitted throughout; some rooms are rope-marked and must not be entered.

schedule.note: Last entry is before closing; event days may restrict access

attractions.verification_note: Ticket and camera charges are revised periodically and the palace closes for private events - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Tipu Sultan's Summer Palace
attractions.summary: A two-storey teak palace of fluted columns and cusped arches, completed by Tipu Sultan in 1791 and now an ASI-protected monument.
attractions.history: Begun under Hyder Ali within the walls of Bangalore Fort and completed by Tipu Sultan in 1791, the structure served as the ruler's summer residence. After Tipu's defeat in 1799 the British used it as the Secretariat of the Mysore administration until 1868. It is built almost entirely of teak, with plastered brick only where structurally necessary.
attractions.significance: The palace is one of the finest surviving examples of Indo-Islamic wooden architecture in southern India and a rare intact civil building associated with Tipu Sultan. Its ground-floor museum holds prints, coins and a replica of Tipu's tiger, and it is protected by the Archaeological Survey of India.
interesting_facts: Tipu is said to have called the palace Rash-e-Jannat - 'the envy of heaven'.
The building is almost entirely load-bearing teak, including the ornamental columns.
Traces of the original floral fresco painting survive on the ceilings and balcony soffits.
The adjacent Venkataramana Temple predates the palace and was deliberately left standing.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The garden and ground floor are approachable, but the upper storey is reached only by a steep wooden staircase.
attractions.photography_policy: Still photography for personal use is generally permitted; tripods and video need ASI permission.
local_customs: Footwear must be removed before stepping onto the wooden floor in some areas - follow the posted signs.

costs.note: Free below 15 years at ASI monuments

attractions.verification_note: ASI ticket rates are revised by notification - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Bangalore Fort (Delhi Gate)
attractions.summary: The surviving stone gateway and bastions of the fort that Kempegowda founded in mud and Hyder Ali rebuilt in stone.
attractions.history: Kempegowda I raised a mud fort here in 1537 as the nucleus of his new settlement. Hyder Ali rebuilt it in stone around 1761, and Tipu Sultan strengthened it further. The fort fell to Lord Cornwallis in March 1791 during the Third Anglo-Mysore War, and most of its walls were dismantled during the nineteenth century as the city expanded. Only the Delhi Gate, a stretch of curtain wall and two bastions remain.
attractions.significance: This is the physical origin point of Bengaluru: the fort defined the old pete (market town) around which the modern city grew. The surviving masonry shows the transition from Vijayanagara-period fortification to the European-influenced bastion design that Hyder Ali's French engineers introduced.
interesting_facts: A plaque near the gate marks the breach through which British forces entered in 1791.
The Ganapathi temple inside the fort walls is still in daily use.
The oval bastions were designed to deflect cannon fire, a French military influence.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The forecourt is level but the ramparts have steep, uneven steps with no railing.
local_customs: The site sits inside a busy wholesale market area - keep valuables secure.

costs.note: Often free; nominal ASI charge may apply

attractions.verification_note: Access hours vary with local market conditions - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Cubbon Park (Sri Chamarajendra Park)
attractions.summary: A 300-acre green lung in the administrative heart of the city, laid out in 1870 and ringed by red-brick colonial institutions.
attractions.history: Laid out in 1870 under Major General Richard Sankey, then Chief Engineer of Mysore, the park was originally named after Sir Mark Cubbon, the long-serving British Commissioner. It was formally renamed Sri Chamarajendra Park in 1927 to mark the silver jubilee of Krishnaraja Wadiyar IV, though the older name remains in daily use.
attractions.significance: Cubbon Park is the civic centrepiece of colonial and post-independence Bengaluru: the High Court, State Central Library, Government Museum and Vidhana Soudha all sit on or around its edges. It functions as the city's principal public space for walking, protest, reading and weekend car-free mornings.
interesting_facts: The park contains around 6,000 trees across roughly 68 genera.
Roads through the park are closed to vehicles on Sundays and public holidays, when it becomes a pedestrian zone.
The bright red Attara Kacheri (High Court) building of 1868 predates the park itself.
The State Central Library inside the park has been in continuous operation since 1915.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Wide, flat, paved paths throughout; accessible toilets near the main entrances. One of the most wheelchair-friendly outdoor spaces in the city.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography allowed; commercial shoots need Horticulture Department permission.
local_customs: Cycling is restricted on some internal paths.

schedule.note: Walking paths open earlier than institutional buildings

attractions.verification_note: Entry is free; timings for buildings inside the park differ.

attractions.name: Vidhana Soudha
attractions.summary: Karnataka's granite legislative building, the largest of its kind in India, floodlit on Sunday and public-holiday evenings.
attractions.history: Built between 1952 and 1956 under Chief Minister Kengal Hanumanthaiah, the building was conceived as a statement that independent India could build in an indigenous idiom rather than a colonial one. Its style, sometimes called Neo-Dravidian or Mysorean Neo-Dravidian, borrows domes, cornices and pillar forms from South Indian temple architecture and renders them in Bangalore granite.
attractions.significance: Vidhana Soudha is the seat of the Karnataka Legislature and the defining civic monument of post-independence Bengaluru. The inscription 'Government's work is God's work' over the eastern entrance is among the most quoted architectural inscriptions in India.
interesting_facts: The building uses granite quarried locally and was constructed partly with prison labour, a fact recorded in contemporary accounts.
The central dome is topped by a four-headed lion capital, the state emblem.
It is illuminated on Sunday evenings and public holidays, which is the best time to photograph it.
Interiors are not open to general tourists; the building is normally viewed from the perimeter.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Viewed from level public footpaths outside the security perimeter.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography from the public road is permitted. Do not photograph security personnel or checkpoints.
local_customs: Interior entry requires official permission; do not attempt to enter without it.

schedule.note: Exterior viewing only; illumination typically on Sundays and public holidays

attractions.verification_note: Exterior viewing only - interior access is not available to general visitors.

attractions.name: ISKCON Sri Radha Krishna Temple
attractions.summary: A large hilltop temple complex combining traditional South Indian gopura forms with glass-and-steel construction.
attractions.history: Opened in 1997 on Hare Krishna Hill in Rajajinagar, the complex was built by the Bangalore chapter of the International Society for Krishna Consciousness. Its design deliberately fuses a traditional Dravidian gopuram and shikhara with contemporary glazed structural elements, a departure from conventional temple construction.
attractions.significance: The temple is one of the largest ISKCON complexes in the world and a major centre of Vaishnava devotional practice in southern India. It also runs the Akshaya Patra mid-day meal programme, one of the largest school feeding operations globally, which began here.
interesting_facts: The complex spans several levels connected by escalators and long ramped walkways.
The Akshaya Patra Foundation, which serves mid-day meals to millions of schoolchildren, was founded from this temple in 2000.
Janmashtami here draws crowds large enough to require managed queueing over many hours.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Ramps and lifts connect all main levels. The walk from the entrance to the main shrine is long, so allow extra time.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress expected - shoulders and knees covered. Footwear must be left at the designated counter.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography and mobile phones are restricted inside the main shrine. Cloakrooms are provided.
local_customs: Leather items are discouraged inside the temple.
Prasadam is offered at the end of the darshan route.
Queues can be long on festival days - plan around them.

costs.note: Free entry; optional paid pooja services

attractions.verification_note: Darshan timings change on festival days - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Bull Temple (Dodda Basavana Gudi)
attractions.summary: A sixteenth-century Kempegowda-era temple housing a monolithic granite Nandi around 4.5 m tall.
attractions.history: Built by Kempegowda I in the Vijayanagara architectural idiom during the sixteenth century, the temple was raised around a single large granite boulder carved into a seated Nandi, the bull mount of Shiva. Local tradition links its founding to an appeal by farmers whose groundnut crops were being damaged, which is also the origin of the annual Kadalekai Parishe groundnut fair held nearby.
attractions.significance: The Nandi here is among the largest monolithic Nandi sculptures in India and the anchor of Basavanagudi, one of Bengaluru's oldest planned neighbourhoods. The Kadalekai Parishe, held every November-December, is a continuously observed agricultural fair with roots several centuries old.
interesting_facts: The idol is said to have been carved from a single boulder already present on the site.
Devotees regularly apply a coating of oil and charcoal, giving the stone its dark sheen.
The annual groundnut fair transforms the surrounding streets into a market for several days.
A separate Dodda Ganapathi temple stands a short walk away and is usually visited together with this one.
attractions.accessibility_notes: A short flight of steps leads to the temple platform; there is no ramp to the inner sanctum.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear must be removed before entering the temple platform.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography of the inner sanctum is generally not permitted; ask before photographing.
local_customs: Remove footwear at the marked line.
Do not step on the threshold of the sanctum.
Offerings are usually flowers, coconut or groundnuts.
attractions.verification_note: Darshan timings vary on festival days - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Visvesvaraya Industrial & Technological Museum
attractions.summary: A hands-on science museum with working engineering exhibits, a Wright Flyer replica and a dinosaur enclosure.
attractions.history: Opened in 1962 and named after the engineer and statesman Sir M. Visvesvaraya, it was among the first science museums established by India's National Council of Science Museums. Its founding brief was to explain industrial technology to a general public through working models rather than static displays.
attractions.significance: The museum is a landmark in Indian science communication and remains one of the country's most visited science centres. Galleries cover engines, electronics, biotechnology, space and a dedicated children's science area.
interesting_facts: The museum houses a full-scale replica of the Wright brothers' 1903 Flyer.
Several exhibits are visitor-operated - you turn the crank and watch the mechanism work.
It runs a rotating programme of science demonstrations and film shows through the day.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Lifts serve all galleries and the entrance is ramped. A strong wet-weather and hot-afternoon option.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography is generally permitted; flash may be restricted in some galleries.
local_customs: Large bags must be left at the cloakroom.

schedule.note: Closed on a small number of national holidays

attractions.verification_note: Ticket prices and show timings are revised periodically - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: HAL Heritage Centre & Aerospace Museum
attractions.summary: India's first aerospace museum, with retired fighters, helicopters, a flight simulator and the story of Hindustan Aeronautics.
attractions.history: Opened in 2001 by Hindustan Aeronautics Limited, the museum traces Indian aviation manufacturing from the founding of Hindustan Aircraft in 1940 through licence production of the MiG-21 to indigenous programmes such as the HF-24 Marut and the HAL Tejas.
attractions.significance: It is the only museum in India dedicated specifically to aerospace manufacturing rather than air-force history, and holds airframes that exist nowhere else in public display, including HAL's own prototypes.
interesting_facts: The HF-24 Marut on display was India's first indigenously designed jet fighter.
Visitors can sit in a cockpit mock-up and try a basic flight simulator for an extra charge.
The outdoor apron holds retired MiGs, a Canberra and several helicopters.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Indoor galleries and the outdoor apron are mostly level; cockpit access requires climbing steps.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography allowed inside the museum. Do not photograph the adjacent HAL airport or operational areas.
local_customs: This adjoins a defence-related facility - follow all posted photography restrictions strictly.
attractions.verification_note: Timings and simulator availability change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: National Gallery of Modern Art, Bengaluru
attractions.summary: Modern and contemporary Indian art shown in the restored Manikyavelu Mansion and a purpose-built new wing.
attractions.history: The Bengaluru branch of the National Gallery of Modern Art opened in 2009 in the Manikyavelu Mansion, an early twentieth-century residence set in about 3.5 acres of grounds. The mansion was restored and paired with a contemporary gallery block to hold larger works.
attractions.significance: The collection traces Indian art from the Bengal School and Raja Ravi Varma through the Progressive Artists' Group to contemporary practice, and is one of only three NGMA campuses in the country.
interesting_facts: The permanent collection includes works by Raja Ravi Varma, Amrita Sher-Gil, Jamini Roy and Rabindranath Tagore.
The old mansion and the new wing are deliberately contrasted in material and light.
The grounds host outdoor sculpture and are a quiet retreat from Palace Road traffic.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The new wing is fully accessible with a lift; the heritage mansion has ramped access to the ground floor.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography inside the galleries is generally not permitted in order to protect the works.
local_customs: Bags must be deposited at the entrance.
Do not touch or lean close to the artworks.

schedule.note: Closed on Mondays and national holidays

costs.note: Free for students with valid ID

attractions.verification_note: Closed Mondays; special exhibition pricing may differ - verify before visiting.

sources.title: National Gallery of Modern Art, Ministry of Culture

attractions.name: Nandi Hills
attractions.summary: A 1,478 m hill fort about 60 km north of the city, famous for sunrise above a sea of cloud and for Tipu Sultan's summer retreat.
attractions.history: The hill was fortified under the Ganga and later Chola periods, and the Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple at its base dates in parts to the ninth century. Hyder Ali and Tipu Sultan strengthened the hill fort in the eighteenth century, and Tipu built a summer residence here. Under the British it became a hot-weather retreat for the Madras and Mysore administrations.
attractions.significance: Nandi Hills is the most accessible high-elevation viewpoint from Bengaluru and an important early-medieval temple and fort site. The Bhoga Nandeeshwara Temple complex at the foot of the hill is protected by the ASI and shows Ganga, Chola, Hoysala and Vijayanagara phases of construction in one place.
interesting_facts: Sunrise inversion layers frequently fill the valley with cloud below the summit, especially between November and February.
'Tipu's Drop' is a sheer cliff face traditionally described as an execution point during Tipu's rule.
The Arkavathi and three other rivers are traditionally said to rise in these hills.
Vehicle entry is restricted on some mornings to manage congestion - check current rules before setting out.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Vehicles can reach near the summit plateau, but viewpoints and the fort involve uneven stone paths and steps. Not suitable for wheelchairs beyond the parking area.
attractions.dress_code: Warm layers for early mornings; the summit is markedly colder than the city.
attractions.photography_policy: Personal photography permitted. Drones require prior permission.
local_customs: Do not feed or approach the resident monkeys.
Carry your waste back down - bins are limited.

schedule.note: Gate timings vary seasonally and on high-traffic days

attractions.verification_note: Access rules, gate timings and vehicle restrictions change frequently - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Ulsoor Lake (Halasuru Lake)
attractions.summary: One of the city's largest surviving tanks, with islands, a boating jetty and a lakeside walking path.
attractions.history: The tank is traditionally attributed to Kempegowda II in the sixteenth century and was substantially remodelled during the British period, when the surrounding cantonment area developed. Like most of Bengaluru's lakes it was originally an irrigation and water-supply tank rather than an ornamental feature.
attractions.significance: Ulsoor is a surviving fragment of the tank cascade system that supplied pre-modern Bengaluru with water, and it illustrates both the ingenuity of that system and the pressure that urbanisation has placed on it. The lake is also a locally important birding spot.
interesting_facts: Several small islands sit within the lake, reachable only by boat.
Bengaluru historically depended on a chain of interconnected tanks rather than a river.
The nearby Someshwara Temple in Halasuru is one of the oldest temples in the city.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The main promenade is paved and mostly level; boating jetty access involves steps.
local_customs: Swimming is prohibited.

schedule.note: Boating operates shorter hours than the walking path

costs.note: Free to walk; boating charged separately

attractions.verification_note: Boating availability varies - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Jawaharlal Nehru Planetarium
attractions.summary: A working planetarium with a hybrid projection dome, a science park and a regular public sky-theatre programme.
attractions.history: Established by the Bangalore Association for Science Education and inaugurated in 1989, the planetarium has run continuous public astronomy programming since. Its projection system has been upgraded over time to a hybrid optical and digital dome.
attractions.significance: It is one of India's most active public astronomy education centres, running school programmes, telescope evenings and a well-regarded science-in-action outdoor exhibit park.
interesting_facts: Shows run in multiple languages on a published daily schedule.
The outdoor Science Park demonstrates physics principles through large climbable exhibits.
Public telescope viewing sessions are organised around notable astronomical events.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Ground-floor access is step-free; the dome auditorium has stepped seating with limited accessible positions - ask staff on arrival.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography is not permitted during dome shows.
local_customs: Latecomers are not admitted once a show has started.

schedule.note: Shows run at fixed times through the day

attractions.verification_note: Show timings, languages and prices change - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Commercial Street & Russell Market Quarter
attractions.summary: The cantonment-era shopping street, backed by the 1927 Russell Market building and a dense food lane.
attractions.history: Commercial Street developed in the late nineteenth century to serve the British cantonment established after 1809. Russell Market, built in 1927 and named after the then municipal commissioner T. B. Russell, remains the anchor wholesale fruit, flower and meat market of the quarter.
attractions.significance: The area preserves the commercial grain of cantonment Bengaluru, distinct from the older pete around the fort. Russell Market's arched brick facade is a protected example of early twentieth-century municipal market architecture.
interesting_facts: The cantonment and the old pete developed as two separate towns and were only merged administratively in 1949.
Russell Market's flower section is busiest before dawn.
The surrounding lanes are known for Ramadan-season night food stalls.
attractions.accessibility_notes: Narrow, crowded and uneven footpaths with parked vehicles; not practical for wheelchair users or those with limited mobility.
attractions.dress_code: No restriction; modest dress is more comfortable in the market lanes.
attractions.photography_policy: Ask before photographing traders and their stalls.
local_customs: Bargaining is normal in the street stalls but not in branded stores.
Keep bags secured in the crowd.

schedule.note: Russell Market opens much earlier; many shops close on Sundays

attractions.verification_note: Shop timings and weekly closures vary - verify before visiting.

attractions.name: Shivoham Shiva Temple
attractions.summary: A modern temple built around a 20 m seated Shiva figure, with a walk-through cave shrine sequence.
attractions.history: Consecrated in 1995, the temple was conceived as a contemporary devotional space rather than a traditional agama-built temple. The monumental Shiva figure, set against an artificial Kailash backdrop with a Ganga cascade, has become a widely recognised city landmark.
attractions.significance: The temple demonstrates a late-twentieth-century pattern in Indian religious architecture: monumental figurative sculpture combined with a designed pilgrim circulation route, aimed at both devotees and casual visitors. The internal cave passage recreates a simplified Amarnath-style darshan experience.
interesting_facts: The seated Shiva figure stands roughly 20 metres tall.
A constructed cave passage leads visitors past a sequence of twelve jyotirlinga representations.
The site is especially busy on Maha Shivaratri, when it stays open through the night.
attractions.accessibility_notes: The main courtyard is level, but the cave passage is narrow with steps and low headroom, and is not wheelchair accessible.
attractions.dress_code: Modest dress. Footwear removed at the entrance.
attractions.photography_policy: Photography of the main figure is usually permitted; the inner cave shrine may be restricted.
local_customs: Remove footwear at the entrance counter.
The cave passage is one-way - follow the marked direction.

costs.note: Free general entry; cave darshan may carry a nominal charge

attractions.verification_note: Timings and any darshan charges are not officially published - verify before visiting.
